title: Signal detective: advanced time series techniques

blocks.content: Compare two generated time series using shared tooltips, legend calculations, and separate axes, then explore scales, flexible bounds, and a zero reference line. You will build and save a dashboard with synthetic practice data from **-- Grafana --**.
Open a new dashboard to begin the lab.
Open the new dashboard page.
blocks.tooltip: Start a fresh practice dashboard.

blocks.content: You have opened a new dashboard for the visualization exercises.
Create a Time series panel with a clear title and two synthetic queries for comparison.
Open **Add** to access the controls for adding a panel.
blocks.tooltip: Open the controls for adding dashboard elements.

blocks.content: In the **Add** pane, click **Panel** to add a panel for the two time series.
blocks.tooltip: Create a place to plot your practice signals.

blocks.content: Select **Edit visualization** to configure the panel and its queries.
blocks.tooltip: Open the visualization configuration.

blocks.content: Select **-- Grafana --** as the data source; the built-in source supplies synthetic data so you can practice without connecting a service.
blocks.tooltip: Generate synthetic data without connecting an external service.

blocks.content: If visualization suggestions are shown, open **All visualizations** and choose **Time series**. Skip this step if the panel options are already shown.

steps.description: Select **All visualizations** to open the visualization choices.
steps.tooltip: Browse the available ways to display data.

steps.description: Select **Time series** to compare how both signals change over time.

blocks.content: In **Panel options**, set **Title** to `Signal detective` to identify the panel.
blocks.tooltip: Give the panel a name that describes its purpose.

blocks.content: Open **Add query or expression**, then choose **Add query** to create query B.

steps.description: Open **Add query or expression** in the query sidebar.
steps.tooltip: Choose what to add to the query list.

steps.description: Select **Add query** to create and select query B.
steps.tooltip: Create a second query for comparison.

blocks.tooltip: Use the same built-in source for the second signal.
blocks.content: Select **-- Grafana --** for query B so both signals use synthetic data.
Click **Refresh** to run both queries and display A-series and B-series.
blocks.tooltip: Run both queries so their signals appear together.

blocks.content: You have used the built-in data source to prepare a named Time series panel for comparing two synthetic signals.
Compare values at one timestamp with a shared tooltip and peaks across the displayed time range with a legend calculation.
In the panel edit pane, open **Tooltip** and set **Tooltip mode** to **All** to compare both series at the same timestamp.
blocks.tooltip: Compare all signals at the same instant.

blocks.content: In **Tooltip**, set **Values sort order** to **Descending** to list the largest value first at each timestamp.
blocks.tooltip: Place the largest value first at the hovered timestamp.

blocks.content: In **Legend**, set **Mode** to **Table** to show summary calculations beside each series.
blocks.tooltip: Make room for per-series summary values.

blocks.content: In **Legend**, set **Values** to **Max** to compare the highest value of each series over the displayed time range.
blocks.tooltip: Find each signal’s peak across the displayed data.

blocks.content: The tooltip compares both values at the hovered timestamp, while **Max** summarizes each series across the displayed data, so their rankings can differ.

blocks.question: Why can the first series in the descending tooltip differ from the series with the largest Max in the legend?

choices.text: The tooltip compares one timestamp; Max summarizes the displayed data.
Opacity gradient changes the data values.
choices.hint: Gradient changes appearance, not the values.

choices.text: Descending sort permanently puts one series first.
choices.hint: The order can change with the hovered timestamp.

blocks.content: Give B-series its own axis, a useful option when signals have different units or very different ranges.

blocks.title: Give one series its own axis

blocks.content: In **Overrides**, click **Add field override**, choose **Fields with name**, then select **B-series** to change only that signal.

steps.description: Select **Add field override** to change one series without changing the panel defaults.
steps.tooltip: Customize a single series without changing the defaults.

steps.description: Choose **Fields with name** to match one exact field name.
Select **B-series** so the override applies only to that signal.
steps.tooltip: Limit this override to the second signal.

blocks.content: For the B-series override, use **Add override property** to add **Axis > Placement**.

steps.description: Select **Add override property** to choose what changes for B-series.
steps.tooltip: Choose which property this override changes.

steps.description: Choose **Axis > Placement** to control which side displays its scale.
steps.tooltip: Control where the selected series scale appears.

blocks.tooltip: Separate the selected series from the default scale.
blocks.content: In the B-series override, set **Axis > Placement** to **Right** so that series has its own scale.
Inspect the preview: B-series should use the right axis while the other signal uses the left; compare their tick labels before comparing line heights.
blocks.tooltip: Compare tick labels before comparing line heights.

blocks.content: Each axis maps its own values to the panel height, so overlapping lines can have different values; read the tick labels or tooltip rather than treating overlap as equal values or proof of correlation.

blocks.question: Two lines now overlap on separate axes. What can you conclude?

choices.hint: Each axis can map a different value to the same height.

choices.text: Read each axis scale before comparing values; overlap alone proves no correlation.

choices.hint: An axis placement change cannot establish causation.

blocks.content: A large spike can flatten smaller changes on a linear scale. Symlog compresses larger magnitudes and stays approximately linear near zero, so it can show both; unlike a logarithmic scale, it supports zero and negative values. The scale changes spacing, not the samples.
Compare how scales display large and small changes, then add flexible bounds and a zero reference line.
In **Axis**, set **Scale** to **Symlog** to compress large magnitudes while keeping zero and negative values visible.
blocks.tooltip: Compare small changes near zero with larger excursions on the compressed scale.

blocks.content: In **Axis**, set **Scale** back to **Linear**: equal vertical distances represent equal absolute changes again.
blocks.tooltip: Restore equal distances for equal absolute differences.

blocks.content: In **Axis**, set **Soft min** to `-100` to give the chart a consistent lower reference while allowing the axis to expand for lower outliers.
blocks.tooltip: Allow lower outliers beyond this preferred bound.

blocks.content: In **Axis**, set **Soft max** to `100` to give the chart an upper reference that can expand for higher outliers; hard bounds can clip values outside the displayed range.
blocks.tooltip: Allow higher outliers beyond this preferred bound.

blocks.content: In **Thresholds**, set **Threshold 1** to `0` as an illustrative reference for values crossing zero; this visual threshold creates no alert rule.
blocks.tooltip: Use zero as an illustrative reference rather than an alert.

blocks.content: In **Thresholds**, set **Show thresholds** to **As lines (dashed)** so the zero reference is visible without covering the signals.
blocks.tooltip: Draw the reference without obscuring the traces.

blocks.content: Click **Back** to view the configured panel in the dashboard.
blocks.tooltip: Inspect the configured panel on its dashboard.

blocks.content: You have compared symlog and linear scales, used soft bounds that preserve outliers, and added a dashed zero reference without creating an alert.

blocks.question: With a soft maximum of 100, what happens if a signal rises above 100?

choices.text: The axis can expand to include the outlier.
The value is always clipped at 100.
choices.hint: A soft bound leaves room for data outside the preferred range.
Axis bounds and visual thresholds do not create alert rules.

blocks.content: Save the dashboard with a recognizable name, then inspect the finished result to confirm the lab configuration is still present.
Save the dashboard as `Time series lab - Signal detective`; this sequence opens the drawer, enters the name, and saves while the drawer covers the guide.

steps.tooltip: Keep your queries and display settings together.
steps.description: Click **Save** to open the save form for the dashboard you just built.

steps.tooltip: Give the practice dashboard a recognizable name.
steps.description: Name the dashboard Time series lab - Signal detective so you can recognize and reuse this practice setup.

steps.tooltip: Persist the dashboard and its panel configuration.
steps.description: Click **Save** to persist the dashboard and its panel configuration.

blocks.content: Inspect the saved dashboard: both signals should appear, the table legend should show **Max**, B-series should use the right axis, and the soft bounds and dashed zero reference should remain configured.
blocks.tooltip: Confirm the saved chart retains every setting you explored.

blocks.content: Saving keeps the two queries and panel configuration together as a reusable dashboard; the finished view lets you check the result.
You can now distinguish timestamp comparisons from whole-range summaries and choose axes, scales, and bounds without confusing their appearance with changes to the data.
